newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish GDP growth seen rising in '97/98 - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Swedish GDP growth seen rising in '97/98 - OECD.

text.p: The Swedish economy will see stronger growth in 1997 and 1998 due to private consumption but inflationary expectations could reignite unless wage growth falls substantially, the OECD said on Monday.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said in its half-yearly report that Swedish gross domestic product (GDP) resumed an upward trend in the first half of 1996, edging up an estimated 1.7 percent for the year.
It forecast GDP would grow by 2.2 percent in 1997 at market prices and 2.1 percent in 1998. Growth will depend increasingly on household demand, which should be helped by lower interest rates.

The OECD warned that high wage growth, running at about six percent in third quarter 1996, could weaken competition and lower profits to the detriment of exports, making the economy vulnerable to a prolonged international slowdown.
The OECD said investment was adding to the productive capacity of Sweden's economy which should be well placed to take advantage of an upswing in Europe.

"However, the real appreciation of the Swedish crown following from the high wage growth and declining productivity growth will gradually feed into loss of market shares at home and abroad," the report said.

"Business fixed investment could, however, be entering a more subdued phase as the high wage growth embedded in the economy weakens competitiveness and lower profits, to the detriment of Sweden's export-market shares."

The OECD said a further fall in interest rates should trigger a replacement cycle in consumer durables and underpin a modest recovery in the housing market. The key repo rate, the central in a three tier system, has fallen to 4.35 percent from 8.91 percent at the start of the year.

Also in 1996 the OECD said Sweden's fiscal consolidation programme was reinforced by additional measures to secure compliance with the Maastricht three percent deficit rule in 1997 and reach a balanced budget in 1998.
"So far the consolidation is progressing as planned," the report said.
